opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tension we think about a lot, and I'd say right now we see the two as complementary more than competing. The honest reality of interpretability today is that it's still a young field. A lot of the most valuable work we do with partners isn't something you can wrap in an API and hand over. It involves sitting with a team, understanding their model and their domain, figuring out which questions are even tractable to ask of the internals, and then iterating. That hands-on engagement is where we learn what actually matters.

So the way I think about it is that the services work is our discovery engine. Every time we go deep with a customer, whether it's a frontier lab, a life sciences company trying to pull new knowledge out of a scientific foundation model, or an enterprise trying to understand why a model is behaving a certain way, we find patterns. We see the same workflows recur: training a sparse autoencoder or some other decomposition, labeling features, finding the circuits behind a specific behavior, doing targeted interventions. Once we've done something by hand three or four times, that's a strong signal it should become product.

Ember, our platform, is really the crystallization of that. The goal is to take what used to need a PhD interpretability researcher and a few weeks, and make it something an ML engineer can do in an afternoon. That's where the leverage is. If interpretability only scales with the number of world-class researchers we can hire, it'll never be the foundational layer we think it should be for AI development.

That said, I'm wary of productizing too early. If you lock in abstractions before you understand the problem, you build the wrong thing, and in a field moving this fast that's a real risk. Methods that were state of the art eighteen months ago already look different. So we try to keep the product opinionated where we have conviction and flexible where we don't.

Longer term, I'd expect the mix to shift a lot toward product. But I don't think the deep research partnerships ever fully go away. The frontier will keep moving, and there'll always be a frontier problem a customer cares about that no tool handles yet. Being in the room for those problems keeps us honest, and it keeps the research and the product pointed at things people actually need.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of the central tensions in how we think about the company, and I don't think we've fully resolved it, which I'd actually argue is the right posture right now.

The way I frame it internally is that the research expertise and the product aren't really competing; the expertise is the pipeline that feeds the product. Every time we go deep with an enterprise customer, say a biotech partner who wants to understand what a protein model is actually representing, or a frontier lab that wants to steer behavior in ways prompting can't reach, we learn something about what interpretability looks like when it has to survive contact with a real problem. That's very different from what you learn writing a paper. The messy parts, the parts where the SAE features don't cleanly map to the thing the customer cares about, the parts where you need a human in the loop to make sense of what the model found, those are exactly the things that tell you what the product has to do.

So the hands-on work is, in a sense, our discovery process. The risk of productizing too early is that you freeze the abstraction before you understand it. Interpretability is still a young enough field that if we had locked in a platform two years ago, we would have built around the wrong primitives.

That said, I'm very aware of the failure mode on the other side, which is becoming a boutique consultancy with a great research team that never scales. Services revenue is seductive because it's real and it comes quickly, but it doesn't compound. And frankly, the mission argument matters here too. If we believe this technology should be in a lot of people's hands, you can't do that with a handful of researchers flying out to customers.

So the discipline we try to hold is pretty simple. We'll take on hands-on engagements, but only where we believe the thing we learn generalizes. If a customer wants something that's bespoke to them and teaches us nothing about the next ten customers, that's a bad deal for us even if it's lucrative. And then internally, every engagement has an explicit question attached: what from this becomes a feature, a workflow, or an API primitive? If the answer is nothing, we probably shouldn't be doing it.

The honest version is that the mix shifts over time. Today it's weighted more toward the expertise. A year or two from now I'd expect that to flip, where the platform does most of the work and the researchers are focused on the frontier cases that push the platform further. But I'd rather get there by letting the product earn its way out of the services work than by declaring victory prematurely.

astra-6.text:
I think the two can reinforce each other. When you work closely with an enterprise customer, you learn which problems actually matter to them and where your tools fall short. That’s valuable feedback for the research, and it helps you figure out what’s ready to become a product.

The tension is that you can end up doing a lot of bespoke work that doesn’t compound. So I’d think about it in terms of what we can reuse: does this engagement help us develop a capability that will be useful to the next ten customers? Can we turn something that requires a researcher today into something a customer can do themselves?

There will still be problems at the frontier where hands-on research expertise is essential. You don’t want to pretend those are solved by putting a nice interface around them. But as the methods mature, more of that work should move into the product. The balance should evolve with what the technology can reliably deliver.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as feeding into each other. When you’re working on a new capability like interpretability, it’s hard to know in advance which parts can become a repeatable product and which parts still require a researcher working closely with a customer. The hands-on work helps you discover that boundary.

The thing you want to avoid is every engagement becoming a completely bespoke research project where nothing carries forward. Ideally, you solve a concrete problem for a customer, learn something about what they actually need, and turn the reusable parts into tools that make the next engagement easier. Over time, the product can take on more of that work, and the researchers can move on to the next unsolved problem.

So I wouldn’t frame the goal as choosing one and abandoning the other. It’s building a loop where working with customers informs the research, and the research becomes something customers can use without needing us in the room every time.
